# Abstract

This gazetteer compiles the population histories of 3694 towns, fortresses and frontier outposts across the 38 historical regions of Eastern Europe and Siberia from 1400AD to the Treaty of Nystad in 1721AD. Spanning Hanseatic ports on the Baltic, Magdeburg-law market towns in Lithuania, Belarus and Ukraine, Muscovite stone citadels, timber forts along the Oka, Belgorod and Simbirsk defence lines, Ural salt and ironworks towns and Siberian river *ostrogi*, the tables trace how war and frontier settlement reshaped urban life over three centuries. While mid-seventeenth-century wars and early eighteenth-century plague cut back the older towns of Lithuania, Belarus, Right-Bank Ukraine and the Baltic coast, new garrison and trading towns grew rapidly across Left-Bank and Sloboda Ukraine, the southern Russian black earth, the Middle Volga, the Urals and Siberia, culminating in the rise of Saint Petersburg after 1703AD.

# Methodology

This gazetteer traces the population history of 3694 towns, fortresses and frontier outposts across the 38 historical regions of Eastern Europe and Siberia between 1400AD and 1721AD: 1.965 in Russia and Siberia (Regions 18-38), 1.184 in Ukraine and Crimea (Regions 9-17), 287 in Belarus (Regions 5-8) and 258 across the Baltic provinces, Lithuania and Old Finland (Regions 1-4) [@Vodarsky1973; @Vodarsky1977; @Kabuzan1963; @Palli1996; @Dunsdorfs1962; @Kiaupa2000; @KarpachevKozlovsky1972; @Yakovenko2006; @Dolgikh1960]. These settlements span Hanseatic ports on the Baltic, Magdeburg-law market towns (*miasteczka*) in Lithuania, Belarus and Ukraine, Swedish border castles in Karelia, Cossack regimental capitals, timber and stone strongholds along the Oka, Belgorod and Simbirsk defence lines, Ural salt and ironworks towns and Siberian river *ostrogi* [@Tikhomirov1962; @Bernotas2013; @Sharukho2010; @Rezun1989; @Zhigalov2024].

Town populations across the benchmark dates are drawn from Baltic ploughland audits (*Hakenrevisionen*) and burgher rolls, the 1528AD Lithuanian muster (*Popis*) and hearth-tax (*podymne*) registers, Muscovite land books (*pistsovye knigi*), the 1646AD and 1678AD household censuses (*perepisnye knigi*), Peter the Great's First Soul Revision (1719-1721AD, *revizskie skazki*), Left-Bank Ukrainian census books (1666AD) and Cossack regimental rolls, Ottoman tax registers (*tahrir defterleri*) for Crimea and Kefe and Siberian fur-tribute (*yasak*) and inspection (*dozornye*) books [@Shapiro1974; @Morzy1965; @Vasiliauskas2012; @Saloheimo1976; @Irtenina2022; @Ozturk2019; @Pokrovsky1984]. Dates before a town was founded or after it was abandoned are marked with a hyphen (-).
